INTERESTS OF AMICI1
The National Homelessness Law Center
(“NHLC”) is a nonprofit organization founded in 1989
and the only national legal advocacy organization
dedicated solely to preventing homelessness. NHLC
uses impact litigation, policy advocacy, and education
to protect the rights of people experiencing or at ris k
of homelessness, and has long focused on the needs of
unaccompanied youth, including LGBTQ+ youth, who
are disproportionately represented among young
people without a safe place to live. NHLC works with
service providers, advocates, and young people across
the country, including those who rely on licensed
youth shelters, and it has a strong interest in
preserving state laws that keep runaway and
homeless youth safe, connect them to supportive
services, and promote family reconciliation whenever
possible.
National Network for Youth (“NN4Y ”) is a
nonprofit organization founded in 1974 by youth
service providers to keep youth in crisis out of juvenile
detention and child welfare systems and to connect
them with comprehensive community-based services.
NN4Y’s mission is to transform systems so that no
young person in America experiences homelessness.
It works in communities with youth who have

experienced homelessness and with service providers

INTRODUCTION
Petitioners ask this Court to open the federal
courts to parents challenging state laws that impose
no obligation on them, have never been applied to
them, and will almost certainly never effect their
families. They describe Washington’s runaway-youth
shelter laws as a scheme to separate children from
loving parents, conceal children’s whereabouts, and
facilitate gender transitions behind parents’ backs.
The laws do none of those things. They reg ulate
licensed youth shelters and Washington’s
Department of Children, Youth, and Families
(“DCYF” or the “Department”). They change only who
notifies a parent when a runaway youth seeking
protected health care arrives at a licensed shelter —
the Department rather than the shelter—and require
the Department to offer voluntary family
reconciliation services and behavioral health
referrals.2 They do not authorize the Department to
take custody of any child, withhold information from
parents, or provide gender-affirming care.3
Amici NHLC and NN4Y work with and on
behalf of the young people these laws exist to protect.

2. Wash. Rev. Code § 13.32A.082(1)(b)(i), (3).
3. See Wash. Rev. Code §§ 13.32A.082(3), 13.34.050,
13.50.100(7).

3


That experience, including providing legal services to
homeless youth and young adults in Washington
State, supplies a perspective missing from
Petitioners’ account. The youth who arrive at licensed
shelters typically have nowhere else to go: whether
they were asked to leave home or told not to come
back, youth fleeing abuse and neglect, or youth whose
families have been fractured by poverty,
incarceration, death, or a caregiver’s mental illness or
substance use. For children whose parents want them
home, the laws are designed to return them as quickly
as possible. Once a parent asks for the child’s return,
a shelter cannot keep the child beyond a short window
absent a court order, 4 and the child’s only practical
alternative to going home is often the street.
Petitioners’ standing theory depends on
ignoring those realities. They posit that the law
creates “concrete incentives” for their children to run
away,5 but no Petitioner alleges that any child knows
the law exists or has run away to a licensed shelter
seeking gender-affirming care.6 Their alleged injuries
arise only if a “convoluted series of events” occurs: a
child runs away, reaches a licensed shelter, declines
immediate reconciliation, tells a shelter worker they

are seeking gender-affirming care within the first 24-
72 hours of arrival, receives and accepts a behavioral
health referral from DCYF, and receives behavioral
health care services.7 The Ninth Circuit unanimously
held that this “enormity of ‘ifs’ and ‘shoulds’” cannot
establish Article III injury.8 It was right.
Nor can Petitioners avoid that conclusion by
declaring themselves the “objects” of the law.9 Unlike
the policies in Mirabelli v. Bonta, 607 U.S. 492 (2026)
(per curiam), which barred schools from telling
parents about their children’s social gender
transitions at school, this law does not aim to
withhold information from parents. Amicus United
States’s argument that Petitioners have a
fundamental right to authority over every step
related to their child’s health care 10 would allow any
parent to challenge any minor -consent law, which
exist in most States.11 Article III does not permit that
result.
SUMMARY OF THE ARGUMENT
Petitioners lack Article III standing because
they allege no actual or imminent injury. Petitioners
are not the “objects” of Washington’s shelter laws,
which regulate only licensed shelters and the
Department and do not require parents to do or

8.  Int'l Partners for Ethical Care Inc. v. Ferguson, 146 F.4th 841,
851 (9th Cir. 2025). Plaintiffs "have not pled current or future
injuries sufficient to confer Article III standing." Id. at 844.
9. See Pet’rs’ Br. Part I.B.
10. U.S. Amicus Br. 2, 12.
11. BIO App. 15a–31a.

5


refrain from doing anything. 12 This Court’s object-ofthe-law cases describe circumstances in which injury,
causation, and redressability are ordinarily obvious;
they do not dispense with the requirement of an
actual or imminent injury. 13 Unlike in Mirabelli ,
where school policy withheld certain information from
parents whose children actually attended those
schools, the laws here change only who notifies
parents, and no Petitioner claims that their children
ever entered a covered shelter. Nor do the laws
regulate parents “through a ‘conduit.’” 14 Petitioners’
asserted current harms are self-inflicted responses to
hypothetical future harm, which do not establish
standing. Petitioners’ theory of future risk depends on
a speculative chain of contingencies, each turning on
the choices of independent actors. Finally, Petitioners’
theory has no limiting principle: it would allow any
parent to challenge any law concerning children
based solely on discontent, worry, and uninformed
conjecture. The judgment should be affirmed.
ARGUMENT
I. WASHINGTON’S SHELTER LAWS ARE A
NARROW SAFETY NET FOR YOUTH
WITH NOWHERE ELSE TO GO, AND
THEIR OVERRIDING GOAL  IS FAMILY
REUNIFICATION.

Each of Petitioners’ standing theories rests on
incorrect assumptions about how these laws operate
and whom they affect. The laws’ purpose, mechanics,
and real -world operation show why Petitioners’
feared injuries are not imminent, likely, or plausible.
A. The Laws Protect Youth Who Have
No Safe Home—Not Children Whose
Parents Want Them Home.
Runaway and homeless youth laws exist to
protect a specific, vulnerable population: young
people who are homeless or have run away, who do
not have a home to return to, or whose parents do not
want them to return. They are not designed for, and
in practice do not serve, children whose parents want
them home. Approxi mately half of so -called
“runaway” youth were in fact forced to leave home or
not allowed to return, 15 and at least a quarter of
unaccompanied youth have experienced abuse and
cannot safely return home.16

children who experience homelessness are more likely
to experience homelessness as adults. 19 Among
callers under 18 to the National Runaway Safeline,
the reported drivers of running away include
emotional or psychological abuse, physical abuse,
neglect, and sexual abuse, as well as household
substance use, witnessing violence, parental
separation, caregiver mental illness, and a family
member’s incarceration. 20 In 2021, 24 percent of

Runaway and homeless youth laws respond to
the reality that adolescents are at heightened risk of
family conflict and dangerous behavior, and they

situations.22 Most youth who run away avoid shelters
and formal systems altogether. 23 Raising barriers to
shelter does not send those youth home; it sends them
to the street, producing the very harm Petitioners
claim to fear —a child whose whereabouts are
unknown and who is beyond any parent’s reach.

B. Federal and State Law Work
Together to Reunify Families.
The federal Runaway and Homeless Youth Act,
34 U.S.C. § 11201 et seq. , governs most programs
assisting runaway and homeless youth. Congress
found that “youth who have become homeless or who
leave and remain away from home without parental
permission, are at risk of developing, and have a
disproportionate share of, serious health, behavioral,
and emotional problems because they lack sufficient
resources to obtain care.” 24 Accordingly, “many such
young people, because of their age and situation, are
urgently in need of temporary shelter and
services….”25 Congress found that such s ervices
should be developed to ensure a sense of safety and
structure, belonging, self -worth and social
contribution, independence and control over one’s life,
and closeness in interpersonal relationships. 26
Programs funded under the Act include emergency
shelter, street outreach, and transitional living
programs for young people who cannot be reunited
with their families, including those fleeing abuse and
neglect.27
Federal law provides a strong foundation, but
providers and youth still confront logistical, legal, and
practical obstacles to accessing shelter and services,
and state law fills those gaps. Minor -consent and
shelter-access laws are common, important tools that

ensure youth can access community-based emergency
shelter and services independent of the child welfare
or juvenile justice systems.28
Washington’s framework has always pursued
one overriding objective: reunification.29 Its laws have
always reinforced the idea that “the experience and
maturity of parents make them better qualified to
establish guidelines beneficial to and protective of
their children.”30 The Legislature sought to increase
children’s safety by preserving families and providing
assessment, treatment, and placement services for
children in need. 31 The ultimate goal is to protect
children whose behavior endangers themselves and to
empower parents with assistance engaging with their
children.32
In 1995, recognizing the “need for services and
assistance for parents and children who are in
conflict,” the Legislature required anyone sheltering

parent, law enforcement, or the State. 33 The next
year, it directed the State, upon receiving such a
report, to “make a good faith attempt to notify the
parent” and to “offer services designed to resolve the
conflict and accomplish a reunification of the
family.”34 That duty, now held by DCYF, remains the
centerpiece of the statute. 35 And the same 2023
legislation Petitioners challenge directs community
support teams to “prioritize reunification between the
youth and the youth’s family to the extent possible
without endangering the health, safety, or welfare of

C. Washington’s Notification
Framework Ensures That Parents
Are Notified.
When a licensed overnight youth shelter takes
in a child it knows is away from home without
permission, it “must contact the youth’s parent within
72 hours, but preferably within 24 hours,” and the
notice “must include the whereabouts of the youth, a
description of the youth’s physical and emotional

youth’s contact with the shelter.” 37 Since 2013, if
“compelling reasons” exist not to notify the parent —
historically, circumstances indicating that
notification would subject the minor to abuse or
neglect—the shelter “must instead notify the
department.”38 The 2023 amendments, enacted as
Engrossed Substitute Senate Bill 5599 (“ESSB
5599”), added a youth “seeking or receiving protected
health care services” to that compelling -reasons
category.39
When the Department receives a shelter’s
report, it “shall make a good faith attempt to notify
the parent that a report has been received and offer
services to the youth and the family designed to
resolve the conflict  including offering family
reconciliation services and accomplish a reunification
of the family.” 40 It must offer those services “as soon
as possible, but no later than three days, excluding
weekends and holidays, following the receipt of a
report.”41 Before ESSB 5599 and Substitute House
Bill 1406 (“SHB 1406”), there was no deadline at all.42
If a youth notifies the shelter that they are seeking
protected health care, the Department must also
“[o]ffer to make referrals on behalf of the minor for
appropriate behavioral health services” and “[o]ffer

Petitioners insist that there is “no guarantee
when or if a parent will learn the fate of their
runaway child.” 44 The statutory framework and
Department’s policies  show otherwise. Parents are
notified either by the shelter upon the child’s arrival
or by the Department when a compelling reason
exists. The Department’s implementing
memorandum requires caseworkers to contact the
youth within twenty -four hours and to “[m]ake  [a]
good faith attempt to contact the youth’s parent or
legal guardian”—at a minimum by asking the youth
or shelter for parent contact information, contacting
the parents, searching the agency’s FamLink records
for prior contact information, and documenting those
efforts.45 Department policy further requires
caseworkers to “[c]ontact the family within twenty -
four hours of being assigned the case.”46
Even when a youth refuses to provide contact
information, other safeguards operate. Every licensed
shelter must check the Washington State Patrol’s
public missing -children information “[a]t least once
every eight hours,” and if the youth is listed as
missing, “must immediately notify the department”
with a description of the youth’s condition and
circumstances—regardless of whether the youth is
seeking protected health care.47 A parent who reports

reunification. The Department may withhold
information about a minor’s whereabouts and
condition only upon determining that release “is
likely to cause severe psychological or physical harm
to the juvenile.” 48 In short, the 2023 amendments
“do[] not deny any information to parents”; they
change “who notifies the parents.”49
D. Notified Parents Retain Every
Right They Had Before.
Once notified by the shelter or the Department,
a parent’s rights are unchanged. Neither a shelter nor
the Department can prevent a parent from taking the
child home. Nothing in ESSB 5599 authorizes the
Department to take custody of a minor because the
minor seeks gender -affirming care; the Department
may take custody only  where a court finds
“reasonable grounds to believe that removal is
necessary to prevent imminent physical harm to the
child due to child abuse or neglect.” 50 The parent
“remains free to pick up their child from a shelter at
any time and the youth remains free to return home,”
whether or not anyone engages in reconciliation
services.51
Nor can the Department require parents to
accept services as a condition of bringing their child

home. Family reconciliation services are, by the
Department’s own policy, “voluntary services
designed to resolve problems related to family
conflict.”52 The statute requires only that the
Department offer referrals and reconciliation
services, which families “can accept or reject.” 53 “[I]f
youth and their parents elect not to undertake
reconciliation services, the Department cannot make
them.”54 And the laws neither direct nor permit the
Department or any shelter to provide genderaffirming care.55
E. The Statutory Design and Practical
Realities Drive Youth Home, Not
Away.
Petitioners’ central premise that the laws make
running away “attractive” ignores how the system
actually works.56 The policy goal and practical reality
are the same: reunifying youth with their families as
quickly as possible.57
First, the statute’s incentives point strongly
toward quick reunification. A minor may authorize
his or her own continued stay in a licensed shelter for

path open from the street to a licensed shelter —and
from the shelter back to the family —are the product
of hard-won experience about what keeps vulnerable
young people alive. Similarly, the importance of laws
that allow certain older minors to consent to some
limited healthcare cannot be overstated. Studies have
found that homeless youth have mortality rates up to
ten times those of their housed peers and suicide rates
anywhere from five to fifteen times those of housed
youth.144 An analysis of Homelessness Management
Information System data found that unhoused
LGBTQ youth had over twice the rate of early
death.145 Exposing every such minor -consent law to
immediate facial challenge by any parent who fears it
would invite the very barriers that the Washington
Legislature found “create additional risk and dangers

CONCLUSION
Petitioners are not the objects of Washington’s
shelter laws, their asserted present harms are self -
inflicted, and their feared future injuries rest on a
speculative chain of contingencies. Because
Petitioners lack Article III standing, the judgment of
the court of appeals should be affirmed.
